statements.radiopharmaceuticals-and-tagging: A radiopharmaceutical is a compound tagged with a radioactive nuclide and chosen because the body sends it to the organ under study. Because $\gamma$ rays pass easily out of the body and a nucleus radiates the same whatever compound it sits in, detectors outside the body can see where the compound has gone.
statements.anger-camera: The Anger camera images a radiopharmaceutical with a lead collimator that passes only $\gamma$ rays traveling along its holes, a scintillator that turns each $\gamma$ ray into light, and photomultipliers that turn the light into a signal. The image it forms is flat and carries no depth.
statements.spect-imaging: Single-photon-emission computed tomography surrounds the patient with detectors and combines their images by computer into a three-dimensional picture, as x-ray CT does for shadows. It gains depth at the cost of resolution.
statements.mass-from-activity: The mass of a radioactive sample follows from its activity and half-life: the activity and half-life give the number of nuclei, and Avogadro's number and the molar mass turn that number into a mass. Medical activities of a few millicuries correspond to astonishingly small masses.
statements.absorbed-dose-rad-and-gray: The absorbed dose is the ionizing energy deposited per kilogram of the tissue affected. It is measured in rad, where $1\;\text{rad} = 0.01\;\text{J/kg}$, or in gray, where $1\;\text{Gy} = 1\;\text{J/kg} = 100\;\text{rad}$.
statements.relative-biological-effectiveness: The relative biological effectiveness (RBE), or quality factor, of a type of radiation is the factor by which its biological effect per unit of absorbed dose exceeds that of x rays. Short-range radiation such as $\alpha$ particles concentrates its damage, which is harder to repair, and so has a large RBE.
statements.dose-equivalent-rem-and-sievert: The dose equivalent is the absorbed dose multiplied by the RBE, a number proportional to the biological effect: $\text{rem} = \text{rad}\times\text{RBE}$ and $\text{Sv} = \text{Gy}\times\text{RBE}$. Dose limits and risks are stated in this quantity.
statements.dose-from-a-source: The dose from a source is found by following its decays into joules per kilogram: the activity and time give the number of decays, the energy per decay gives the energy deposited, the mass of tissue gives the dose in grays, and the RBE gives the dose in sieverts. Activity is not to be confused with dose along the way.
statements.immediate-effects-and-dose-levels: A single whole-body dose below about 0.1 Sv has no observable immediate effect, a dose near 1 Sv causes radiation sickness, and a dose near 5 Sv is fatal to about half of those who receive it. Blood counts fall first because blood cells reproduce fastest.
statements.linear-hypothesis-and-long-term-risk: The linear hypothesis assumes that the risk of a radiation-induced cancer is proportional to the dose, even at doses too low for any effect to be observed. Scaling down from high doses in this way gives about $10/10^{6}\;\text{rem}\cdot\text{y}$ for the risk of cancer.
statements.background-radiation: Everyone receives background radiation, about 3 mSv a year on average, from cosmic rays, from rocks and soil, from the body's own nuclides and, above all, from radon. Its size varies from place to place and is the natural yardstick for every other dose.
statements.radiation-protection: A dose is limited in only three ways: by keeping the time of exposure short, by increasing the distance from the source and by placing shielding between the source and the body.
statements.free-radicals-and-radiolytic-products: Ionizing radiation makes free radicals in food and in organisms, and their reactions produce new compounds called radiolytic products. Free radicals are how irradiation kills organisms, and the radiolytic products are the center of the debate about the safety of irradiated food.
statements.coulomb-barrier-to-fusion: Two positive nuclei repel each other until they come close enough for the short-ranged nuclear attraction to take over. Their potential energy is therefore a hill, the Coulomb barrier, with a deep well at its center.
statements.proton-proton-cycle: The Sun shines by the proton-proton cycle, three reactions in which four protons and two electrons become a helium nucleus, two neutrinos and six $\gamma$ rays: $2e^{-} + 4\,{}^{1}\text{H} \to {}^{4}\text{He} + 2v_{\text{e}} + 6\gamma$, releasing 26.7 MeV. The first two reactions must happen twice for each helium nucleus made.
statements.fusion-energy-from-a-mass-of-fuel: The energy from fusing a given mass of fuel is the number of reactions in that mass times the energy per reaction, and dividing the energy by the time over which it is released gives the average power.
statements.magnetic-and-inertial-confinement: Magnetic confinement holds a hot, thin plasma for a long time in a magnetic field, as in a tokamak, while inertial confinement compresses a dense fuel pellet with laser beams for a very short time. The two techniques trade density against confinement time.
statements.fission-energy-from-masses: The energy released by a fission is the mass destroyed times $c^{2}$, found from the atomic masses of the reactants and of the products, with the neutrons counted among the products.
statements.neutron-induced-fission: In neutron-induced fission a neutron, having no charge, enters a heavy nucleus at low energy and deposits enough energy to set it oscillating like a struck drop until Coulomb repulsion splits it into two fragments and a few neutrons: $n + {}^{A}\text{X} \to \text{FF}_{1} + \text{FF}_{2} + xn$.
statements.fission-energy-per-kilogram: The energy from fissioning a given mass of fuel is the number of nuclei in that mass times the energy per fission. Each fission gives ten times the energy of a fusion, but a kilogram of fission fuel gives only about a quarter as much as a kilogram of fusion fuel, because it holds far fewer nuclei.
statements.breeding-plutonium: Breeding turns ${}^{238}\text{U}$ into fissile ${}^{239}\text{Pu}$: the ${}^{238}\text{U}$ captures a neutron, and the ${}^{239}\text{U}$ formed decays by two $\beta^{-}$ decays through ${}^{239}\text{Np}$. Breeding makes the other 99 percent of natural uranium usable, and it makes bomb material.
statements.nuclear-weapon-energy-output: The yield of a nuclear weapon is stated in kilotons or megatons of TNT and corresponds to a mass destroyed of a few grams to a few kilograms. Its energy goes into blast, thermal radiation and nuclear radiation in proportions unlike those of a conventional explosive.

new.name: Tagged compound
new.statement: A compound is tagged when a radioactive nuclide is attached to it, so that the nuclide's radiation shows where the compound goes.

new.name: The rad, $1\;\text{rad} = 0.01\;\text{J/kg}$
new.statement: The rad, short for radiation absorbed dose, is the dose that deposits 0.01 J of ionizing energy in each kilogram of tissue.

new.name: The gray, $1\;\text{Gy} = 1\;\text{J/kg}$
new.statement: The gray is the SI unit of absorbed dose, the dose that deposits 1 J of ionizing energy in each kilogram of tissue; one gray is 100 rad.

new.name: The rem, $\text{rem} = \text{rad}\times\text{RBE}$
new.statement: The rem, short for roentgen equivalent man, is the unit of dose equivalent that goes with the rad: a dose in rad times the RBE of the radiation gives the dose equivalent in rem.

new.name: The sievert, $1\;\text{Sv} = 1\;\text{Gy}\times\text{RBE}$
new.statement: The sievert is the SI unit of dose equivalent: a dose in grays times the RBE of the radiation gives the dose equivalent in sieverts, and one sievert is 100 rem.

new.name: Low dose
new.statement: A low dose is a dose of less than about 0.1 Sv (10 rem), below which no immediate effect can be observed.

new.name: Moderate dose
new.statement: A moderate dose is a dose from about 0.1 Sv to 1 Sv (10 to 100 rem), which can cause measurable changes in the blood and, near the top of the range, radiation sickness.

new.name: High dose
new.statement: A high dose is a dose greater than about 1 Sv (100 rem), which causes radiation sickness and, at several sieverts, can be fatal.

new.name: Hormesis
new.statement: Hormesis is the proposal that a very low dose of radiation may be beneficial, stimulating the body's repair mechanisms; the evidence for it is not conclusive.

new.name: Shielding
new.statement: Shielding is a layer of material placed between a radiation source and the body to absorb the radiation and so reduce the dose.

new.name: Radiotherapy
new.statement: Radiotherapy is the use of ionizing radiation to treat disease, above all to destroy cancer cells.

new.name: Free radicals
new.statement: Free radicals are molecules or atoms with an unpaired electron, made when ionizing radiation breaks molecular bonds; they are highly reactive.

new.name: Radiolytic products
new.statement: Radiolytic products are the compounds produced in food by the chemical reactions of free radicals that irradiation creates.

new.name: Nuclear fusion
new.statement: Nuclear fusion is a reaction in which two nuclei combine to form a larger nucleus.

new.name: Break-even
new.statement: Break-even is the point at which a fusion reactor produces as much energy from fusion as is put into heating and confining its fuel.

new.name: Ignition
new.statement: Ignition is the point at which the fusion in a reactor produces enough energy to keep the fuel hot and fusing without any further energy put in.

new.name: Magnetic confinement
new.statement: Magnetic confinement is the technique of holding a hot fusion plasma away from the walls of its container with magnetic fields, as in a tokamak.

new.name: Inertial confinement
new.statement: Inertial confinement is the technique of compressing and heating a small pellet of fusion fuel so quickly, usually with laser beams, that it fuses before its own inertia lets it fly apart.

new.name: Nuclear fission
new.statement: Nuclear fission is a reaction in which a nucleus splits into two or more smaller nuclei.

new.name: Fission fragments, $\text{FF}_{1}$ and $\text{FF}_{2}$
new.statement: The fission fragments are the two daughter nuclei into which a nucleus splits in fission.

new.name: The liquid drop model
new.statement: The liquid drop model treats a nucleus as a drop of nuclear matter: energy deposited in it sets it oscillating and deforming, and when it deforms far enough the Coulomb repulsion of its two ends overcomes the short-ranged nuclear attraction and it splits.

new.name: Critical mass
new.statement: The critical mass is the minimum mass of fissile material needed for a self-sustained chain reaction.

new.name: Criticality
new.statement: Criticality is the condition in which, on average, exactly one neutron from each fission goes on to cause another fission, so the chain reaction proceeds at a steady rate.

new.name: Supercriticality
new.statement: Supercriticality is the condition in which, on average, more than one neutron from each fission goes on to cause another fission, so the chain reaction grows.

new.name: Breeder reactor
new.statement: A breeder reactor is a reactor designed to make more fissile fuel, such as ${}^{239}\text{Pu}$ from ${}^{238}\text{U}$, than it consumes.
